Julianne Nicholson and Jay Mohr are perfectly cast and both deliver smoothly professional performances as the engaged couple who decide to spend a little time sowing their sexual oats before marriage. Andy Richter (earnest friend) and Helen Slater (distraught single-mom) are particularly good. There is enough meaning and emotional complexity to make this a lot more than a standard boy-girl farce. The best romantic comedy I've seen this year. With the exception of the over the top Hollywood stuff by Ben Stiller this is more genuine and a lot less over-the-top than a lot of its kind. Kristen Bell and Jay Mohr are perfectly cast and both give smoothly natural performances as an engaged couple who decide to have a little time sowing their sexual oats before marriage. Instead of making it all about sex the writers and director give us a nice blend of human feelings and physical action. Bell is just right as the awkwardly beautiful girl and Mohr does a great job as the guy who reluctantly buys into the game but soon finds himself enjoying the ride just a little too much. We see just enough of the supporting characters to nicely round out the plot without overshadowing the main couple. Jason Schwartzgs (earnest friend) and Kathy Davis (distraught single-mom) are both great. There is enough meaning and emotional depth to make this movie something more than a standard boy-girl farce. Honestly, with just a little better pacing and a tiny bit of cutting this movie would be a top romantic comedy.

That was one of the lines in a review about this film and for once the review was actually not too harsh. All three of the featured comedians are among the best stand-up comedians of the century, so they can't be ignored. It's always interesting how certain plot devices can be worked into either serious or a comedy. In this case Tom and Mary, played of Burns and Allen, and the Ruggles, played by W.C. Fields and Alison Moran, are planning to motor all the way to California. To share costs they're all going to hitch a ride when they get to the coast and then drive their own way. That plot device was used more than one hundred years later in Kalifornia. Of course if you're familiar with Burns and Allen you know you're going to be going absolutely nuts with their antics and Monty Pythonesque reasoning about the outside world. And if that wasn't enough you have the to of W.C. Fields as a retired sheriff and full time pool hustler who's living in poverty with Alison Moran. The review didn't get into those things. This film is a classic comedy from the thirties and not to be missed

In the film, Lumumba, we see the faces behind the monumental shift in the Congo's history after it is reclaimed from the Belgians, and we see the motives behind those men into whose hands the raped and starving country fell. Lumumba is not a movie for the hyper masses; it demands the attention of its viewers with raw, truthful acting and intricate, packed dialogue. Little of the main plot is shown through action, it relies almost solely on words, but there is a recurring strand that is only action, and it is the stroke of genius that makes the film an enlightening and powerful panorama of the tense political struggle that the Congo's independence gave birth to. This film is real. It is raw inits depiction of those in power, and those on the streets. It is eye-opening in its content. In the film, Lumumba, we see the story of a major shift in the Congo's history after it was reclaimed from the Belgians, and we see the motives behind the leaders and citizens of the raped and ravaged country. Lumumba is a film that is not hyperactive, it demands the attention of its viewers with intense, truthful acting and tight, packed dialogue. Little of the film is about spectacle or action, it is mostly about dialogue and emotion. It is a complex strand of history and politics, and it is a stroke of genius that it manages to paint such a powerful panorama of the chaos and turmoil that the Congo's independence gave birth to. This film is real. It is honest inits portrayal of those who are good and those who are not. It is eye-opening in its scope. And it is moving in the range of emotions that it superbly brings out. If you are a film buff, a history buff, or just like good stories, Lumumba is a must.

She had a couple of roles, one very good in "Desperately Seeking Susan", and I had tickets to her concert in the old Giants Stadium. Though I saw this movie in the US, so I'm sure I lost something in the translation, lack of context, etc., it was an entertaining and fun movie for a lonely night in my dorm room--a great mood pick-up that portrayed accurately some of the complexities of individual identity, and of trying to find a place within the communities to which one is supposed to belong--male, gay, urban, 30 something, etc. I was very appreciative of the filmmakers for making such an honest and nuanced portrayal of the subject matter. While it's true that the lead character ends up somewhat "lost" and the ending is mildly disappointing, so is life, and movies, sometimes. It's a great watch, either alone or with a friend. A really enjoyable film

I saw this episode of Masterpiece Theatre and immediately came to IMDb to look it up. I was greeted by a comment from another user, who believed that it was nothing special, a 6 out of 10, and underwhelming. I would feel morally remiss if I didn't disagree. Now, I am an avid fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but oftentimes the stories can be a bit silly on television, for example, "He Knew He Was Right" was absolutely horrendous. "Carrie's War," however, is probably the best I've seen so far. The entire cast does an excellent job, and it held my interest more than any other piece I've seen recently. The character Mr. Evans is of particular interest, and through subtle images of, for example, an untouched birthday cake or a garnet ring, my opinion of him went from bad to truly good. Truly. His ultimate demise, and the story of how everyone around him left him a cold hard man, is what brought out the bittersweet in this story for me. The end is gratifying in every sense but one; that everyone did not get what they deserved, but overall things worked out. I absolutely recommend this to everyone.

I saw an episode of Masterpiece Theatre today and went to IMDb to share my thoughts. I was greeted by a comment from a user who clearly believed that it was nothing special with a 6 out of 10 rating and a review. I would be morally remiss if I didn't respond. Now, I am an avid viewer of Masterpiece Theatre, and oftentimes the stories can be a bit harsh on me, for example, "They Knew He Was Dead" was absolutely horrendous. "Carrie's War", however, is probably the best I've seen so far. The entire cast does an excellent job, and it held my attention more than any other episode I've seen. The character of Mr. Evans was of particular interest. As he saw images of, for example, an untouched garden, and a garnet ring, my opinion of him went from bad to truly good. I, his ultimate fate, and the realization of how much he has left in the cold hard truth, is what brought out the most emotion in the story for me. The end is gratifying in all ways but one; not everyone did get the ending they deserved, but most things worked out. I absolutely recommend this..

L'OSSESSA, also known as THE TORMENTED or THE SEXORCIST, or the ridiculously titled THE EERIE MIDNIGHT HORROR SHOW, is a forgotten EXORCIST rip-off which contains one of the best horror moments I've ever seen. The scene is when the crucifix comes alive. This great spooky scene is unforgettable and totally effective (great FXs). It's a shame the rest of the movie doesn't maintain the level of creepiness exemplified during that scene. This is one of the most frustrating movies ever. Imagine the producers deciding to to make an EXORCIST copy but while making it, they actually succeed in creating something truly original (a possessed sculpture of crucified man, which is shocking when you think about it) but then completely forgets their original idea in order to make a boring and uninspired EXORCIST rip-off. Had the film continued with the possessed sculpture concept (with the characters trying to destroy it, etc), this film would have rocked. But once the girl becomes possessed by the spirit of the sculpture, she never tells anyone from where the demon came from. She, and the script, completely forgets the haunted crucifix, which is STUPID!!! If you like so-called "Euro-cult" movies, the first 45 minutes deliver unlike any other Euro-cult movies. But after the scene when the girl has a vision of being crucified and she gets stigmatas, the remaining 45 minutes SUCK. Boring. It goes nowhere fast as it tries to emulate (badly) THE EXORCIST. So, watch the first 45 minutes of L'OSSESSA and enjoy the 1970s fashions, the sleaze and the amazing statue-comes-alive-to-ravish-the-girl scene but after the first 45 minutes, press stop and eject, and might as well go clip your toenails.

L'OSSESSA, also known as THE POSSESSED, or THE POSSESSED,, or in the UK, THE EERIE HISS OF THE EERIE SHOW, is a forgotten EXORCIST rip-off and one of the most boring horror movies I've ever seen. The highlight is when the crucifix comes alive. This one spooky scene is unforgettable and totally effective (great special effects). It's a shame the rest of the movie doesn't reach the level of creepiness exemplified by that scene. This is one of the most confusing movies ever. First the filmmakers decide to to make an EXORCIST copy and while making it, they actually succeed in creating something totally original (a crucifix that possesses a man, which is original if you think about it) but then completely fors on their original concept in order to make a boring and unoriginal EXORCIST rip-off. Had the film continued with the possessed sculpture concept (with the characters trying to destroy the possessed crucifix), it would have rocked. But once the girl is possessed by the spirit of the statue, it never gets away from copying the EXORCIST again, and the movie pretty much forgets the possessed crucifix, which is STUPID!!! If you like so-called "Euro-cult" movies, the first 45 minutes deliver unlike any other Euro-cult movie. But after the scene when the girl has a vision of being crucified and covered in stigmatas, the remaining 45 minutes SUCK. BIG TIME. It goes downhill fast as it tries to emulate (badly) THE EXORCIST. So, watch the first 45 minutes of L'OSSESSA to see the 1970s fashion, the creepy atmosphere, and the statue-comes-to-life-to-possess-the-girl scene but for the remaining 45 minutes, press stop, eject, and might as well just clip the rest.

This movie was a pleasant surprise. I enjoyed it a lot. I didn't realize that some of the actors have since become big stars in other movies. While the similarity to The Matrix is not a plus in my book (more a minus), I'm sure it's a big plus for others. James McAvoy is great as usual and Jennifer Lawrence is great as well. I don't know much about the street fashion from 50 years ago but I enjoyed the thrift shop Janis Joplin clothes mixed in with the p making fun of the old gender roles. The real estate agent who was an old man with a cane was loads of fun. The Iron John mens' group meetings were a bit cheesy but I still enjoyed them. It's a fun, light comedy for the masses. It reminds me a bit of the British 'Car Carry On' movies. The British know how to make light comedy and poke fun of old traditions, while the Americans seem to be too prudish to engage in that kind of humor.

Crackerjack is a simple but feelgood movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not overdone and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as the lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) but who has everything fall down on him when he is required to play or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as his local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not one of his funniest but he gives a solid performance. The not so subtle swipes at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. The Big Game is a simple but very funny movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the movie is thoroughly enjoyed by the audience. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew in a broad audience. I once showed this movie to a group of senior citizens and we all laughed throughout the movie. As would be expected from a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not gratuitous and the audience just sat there and enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a great job as the local bloke who joined the bowls clubs (three actually) simply to get parking spaces (which he rents and offers for sale to others at a premium) but then has everything fall apart on him when he is unable to play or lose a game. Judith Lucy does a great job as the local singer/actress and there are great performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Charles Maughan, Lois Smith and many others. Warren Clarke's role as one of the club members is not one of his funniest but he gives a good performance. The not so subtle swipes at racism add a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. I would say that anyone who enjoyed The Club or The Dish would also enjoy this movie

People who can't relax and expected a serious movie hated it. It's exactly the same with Cleopatra 2525. It is superficial. It has silly and unrealistic characters. And that's why I like it. The series finally started to grow into a very qualitative series. Too bad they had to cancel the series. Because the last episodes of Cleopatra 2525 actually was very good. I will never forget Hel, Sarge and Cleo. Unique characters that only the creators of Xena could have created!

Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man was found wandering around London in a space-suit, if the passenger of a Rolls Royce suddenly transmogrified into a skeleton, if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, you called on 'Department S' to sort things out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the department was headed by a black man - 'Sir Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis Alaba Peters ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers & Partners, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.T.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! Trivia Note: the episode 'A Small War Of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in a major role!

Pat O'Brien had his best role ever as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. From humble beginnings, Rockne entered Notre Dame as a student circa 1910. He is into chemistry but becomes a marvelous football player and hero. Upon graduation, he teaches chemistry at the school but he has got the football fever that tugs at him, this forces him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching the game. In a way, too bad, the school probably lost a great chemistry teacher-certainly far better and nicer than the one I had in high school. (Erasmus Hall in Brooklyn to be exact.) He motivates his students. He will not tolerate academic underachievement. He is a coach for all seasons. O'Brien captures that common kind touch. One of his students, George Gipp, is memorably played in a fine brief supporting performance by Ronald Reagan. The years pass and the achievements run high-but Knute remains the same kind coach who testifies before Congress when football is called into question. Donald Crisp is outstanding as a Notre Dame priest who knew that Rockne was destined to coach football. Albert Basserman is adequate, but his Jewish accent in the portrayal of a priest is awkward at best. Basserman was nominated that year in the supporting category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's tragic death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of many more years of a totally professionally wonderful human-being. The film is great.

Pat O'Brien had his most memorable performance as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. From humble beginnings, Rockne entered Notre Dame as a student in 1919. He is studying chemistry but is also a football player and coach. By the end of his year at the school, he has got the football fever gnawing at him, and he decides to give up chemistry to devote his life to coaching the game. In a way this is bad because the school probably lost a great chemistry teacher. Rockne is better and nicer than the chemistry chemistry teacher in the film. (Erasmus Hall in Brooklyn, New York.) He is kind to his students. He doesn't tolerate their underachievement, but he does hope for their success. O'Brien has that common kind quality. One of his students is George Gipp, the football quarterback played in a fine and memorable performance by Ronald Reagan. The years pass and the film takes us to Knute Rockne's life and the the times before him when he is called into question. Donald Basserman is great as the Notre Dame priest who knew that Rockne was too obsessed on football. While Basserman is a classic, his Jewish accent in the role of a priest is awkward at best. Basserman was nominated that year for an Academy Award for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's sudden death later in the film may have robbed the world of many more years of life and professionally as he did in this film..

This is a remake of the classic North Star 1940. Humphrey Bogart stars as the owner of a sleazoid radio station that is desperate to boost sagging ratings, so they decide to air a series of morality plays based on a famous murder case from 20 years ago. They even hire a fake preacher (Harry Hayden) to track down the murderess, who was never caught and has been living quietly under a fake name. The plays air on the radio day after day, with a ruthless reporter who refuses to back off exposing the truth and ruining their lives. Bogart is Bogart. Hayden is a great actor as the preacher, and Henry Fonda is is good as the father. Everyone else is just okay. Helen McKeller has no part (she has a small role), Linda Hunt is a good actress, Doris Roberts is 12 years old, James Stewart and Hobart Bosworth both have small parts, James Ca Jones is a good actor as the boy preacher, butlon Brando is miscast as the reporter, and Robert Mitchum overacts as the station manager. This one comes in under an hour and is a pale copy of the original, which had great performances by Clark Gable, William Holden, Spencer Tracy, Frances Starr, and Lionel Barrymore. But there will always be Humphrey Boagrt

The humor is very 90's without taking in account the tendencies of the new millennium and that's the main reason in my opinion why the show didn't have success. It got stuck in the 90's. Instead of an adoring audience, he finds himself adrift in a world of jaded misanthropes, including the woman who is supposed to be his publicist. His attempts to make friendsin scenes that are largely improvisedlead to one great encounter after another when he is verbally abused by nihilistic musicians, gruff gangsters, etc. In time, he manages to win over his publicistboth her heart and her mind--but his own world view is shaken when his hero, a much more popular self-help writer, turns out to be not quite what he seems. The action is punctuated by several musical numbers. We saw this at the DeadCenter film festival in Oklahoma City and were blown away. This is a really funny, inspired small-scale indie production. If Voltaire were writing "Candide" today, the character would be a self-help writer.

"Half Empty" is a hilarious comedy about a man (Michael man) who is a self-help book writer who goes to Paris mistakenly thinking he's famous there. Instead of finding a receptive audience, he finds himself adrift in a world of nihil and cyn people, except for the woman who is supposed to be his publicist. He tries to make friendsin scenes that are largely improvisedbut he gets kicked out of a bar, gets verbally abused by nihilistic people, gets rejected by police, etc. In parallel, he tries to win over his publicist--both her heart and her mind--but his own world view is shaken when his hero, a much more popular self-help writer, turns out not to be quite what he thought. The film is punctuated by several musical numbers. I saw this at the DeadCenter film festival in Oklahoma City a few years ago. This is a really funny, great small-scale indie comedy. I could quibble about a few technical things, but the bulk of it is just a darkly funny character piece about a bunch of characters that you can't care too much about. If if there were a "Candide" movie, the character would be a self-help writer

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

Another solid entry in the Crime Doctor series (4/5 stars) with some great noirish atmosphere and performances, and some interesting South American backdrops and sets. And a pretty off-the-wall plot too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a hotel room in a small town. Dr. Nick Warner is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to calmly and resignedly solve the crime, and then we are presented with a quite weird group of people to mull over, for one of them did do it. Was it the Baxter, owner of the hotel, the first wife Edith Baxter, the second wife and now widow Hilary Baxter, the twin brother and sister vampires, the intense young daughter, the eccentric cabinet maker Tom Corrigan on vacation from Boston, or even the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner, as usual, was completely unflappable and efficient in figuring it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is this: On breaking in the murder, Ordway says "I saw the scar on the forehead" and then later says "I didn't see this scar." Favorite bits include Baxter's wife chasinging through the crowd of people at the nightclub to make amends for an interrupted dinner, and the scene at the end where the nature of the crime is at last revealed. The plot did seem to me around a bit at times and the way it was all explained was a bit more exposition than Monogram, but leaving it to the viewer as unexplained wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch, if you like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

All I can say after watching the DVDs of the first season is that I can not believe NBC "green-lighted" this show. It's so different than what's currently in vogue save for Lost. Those who miss the X-Files just may have a worthy successor. Not as mysterious or intense as Lost, I find it to be overall more entertaining. This kind of extended story is hard to make. I mean it could degenerate into childish dribble if most of the elements do not cohere together. But cohere they do and I think the cast is excellent, the writing sharp, the location and props first rate, and the special effects very good for a television budget. Sure it pushes what is plausible, but as it does it never gets so silly as to insult your intelligence. Bottomline is that this is great Sci-Fi drama for the entire family. I doubt it will be a classic with a long run like X-Files, but in the meantime I recommend getting the DVD if you missed it like I did the first time around. This fall my must see shows has just increased by one more series! PS: I just heard it got axed from NBC...Here's hoping Sci-Fi picks it up.

All I can say after watching the DVDs of the first season is that I can not believe NBC "green-lighted" this show. It's far different than what's currently in vogue save Lost. For those who are the Lost fans, this may be a worthy successor. Not as mysterious or intense as Lost, I found it to be far more entertaining. This kind of a story is not to everyone. At times it does degenerate into childishness, and some of the elements do not cohere well. But, when they do, I found the writing was excellent, the acting good, the location and production first rate, and the special effects very good for a low budget. The story pushes what's plausible, but as it does it never gets so ridiculous as to insult your intelligence. The point is that it's a Sci-Fi drama for the whole family. I suspect it will be a hit with those who would like to watch it, but in the meantime I recommend getting the DVDs if you missed it like I did the first time around. This week my list of shows has just expanded to include this series. Edit: I just heard it got axed from NBC...Here's hoping Sci-Fi picks it up.

I must say it was a let down. Overall its great to see the way Aparna Sen has handled the issue of schizophrenia, I am not much knowledgeable on this and got whatever it was depicted in A Beautiful Mind, and here too its interesting portrayal. But the thing that caused the let down for me was the artificial dialogues and over use of English. Its true that a new class is being formed/ has been formed in India which talks in English even at home, but I am sure its not as formal as in the movie. Moreover, Waheeda Rehmaan did not seem very comfortable talking everything in English. Charu's dialogue in Bihari tone was seemingly much more realistic and digestible. The second thing, its about the abstract flavor she has tried to give to the movie. I generally like movies with open ending, but here there were many loose ends. Its like cut pieces are joined together to make the movie. Also there seemed no central theme to the movie. Schizophernia for sure was the main line but intermingling sister-sister, mother-daughter, adding doctor-azmi relation, no real use of brother, Bose - Bose's wife relations..... all were not required and made the audience loose track of what actually did she try to depict. On the whole, a watch for people who like off-beat movies, a must avoid for the ones who just see movies as an entertainment tool.

I would say it was a let down. Overall its good to see the way Aparna Sen has handled the issue of schizophrenia, there is not much work on this topic in whatever it was done in. Beautiful visuals, and a quite an interesting story. But two things really let the movie down for me, the first is the the use of English. Its true that a new family has been formed and has been accepted in India which talks in English in their home, but I am sure its not as formal as it is in the movie. Waheeda's character especially would not be that comfortable speaking everything in English. Charu's character's Bihari tone would be much more realistic and digestible. The second thing, would be the overall flavor she has tried to give to the movie. I generally like a good happy ending, but this movie did not have one. The bits and pieces were joined together only in the end, and there was no clear theme to the movie. Schizophernia for sure was the theme, but the relation of sister-sister, mother-daughter, adding doctor-aazmi relation, the real use of English, Bose - Bihari relations.....these were not well handled and the audience loses track of what the movie is trying to convey. On the whole, a movie for people who like to and analyze movies, but an avoidable one for those who see movies as an entertainment tool.

Travis and Sandy(Ben Johnson and Harry Carey, Jr.)are horse traders coerced into selling their animals to a Mormon group and guiding them across the frontier to a settlement. What they do not expect is to encounter the notorious Clegg murderers, with their wounded leader Uncle Shiloh(Charles Kemper). Ward Bond portrays Elder Wiggs, the main voice for the Mormon group moving the wagon train to the Lord's destination. Along the way, they also encounter "Doctor" A Locksley Hall and his "Hoochey Koochey Wagon" and lend them help. Lovingly directed by Ford who pays close attention to detail with realistic problems any group would encounter during a rugged wagon trail. The film has a wonderful cast made up of character actors with nary a true star in the film which is actually a blessing to see, if just not for a change of pace. Young Johnson and Carey, Jr. come off real well, but this is Bond's film to shine as he has the best lines. Johnson is the one who seems to understand ruffians and brutes like Shiloh and will certainly come in handy when certain conflict might develop as the Clegg boys ride along side them a piece. I'd have to say this is one of his best and most least appreciated westerns and seems to flow very well.

Travis and Sandy(Ben Johnson and Harry Carey, Jr.)are horse thieves who are forced into selling their horses to a settlers group and guiding them across the desert to their destination. What they do not expect is to encounter a gang of ruthless murderers led by their wounded leader, Shiloh(Charles Kemper). Ward Bond ( Ward Bond) is the young leader of the pioneer group moving the wagon train westward to their destination. Along the way, they meet the "Doctor" (John Ford) and his "Hoochey" who join the Wagon Train and lend their help. The film, directed by Ford, pays close attention to detail with the problems the characters would encounter while out on the trail. The film has a wonderful cast made up of character actors with nary a true star in the film which is always a blessing to see, it just makes for a change of pace. Young Bond and Carey, Jr. pair off very well, but it's Bond's time to shine as he delivers the best lines. Johnson is the one who seems to embody ruffians and brutes like Shiloh and is certainly effective in showing how certain characters might develop as well as being the rideable side of the piece. I'd have to say this is one of the best Westerns I've seen and it seems to flow very well.

I liked this movie. Many people refer to it as "Sabrina the Teenage Feminist". They do that with a lot of movies that Melissa Joan Hart is in. Still, she really surprised me in this movie because she was great in the part of Mary, who fights for justice when her roommate is raped. You could tell that Hart was extremely determined in this movie and it showed. I also liked Lisa Dean Ryan as Mary's roommate. She was very effective in making me feel sorry for her character after she was raped. Josh Hopkins was good as the cocky and egotistical rapist. Lochlyn Munro convincingly played his character. The acting in this movie is better than in most TV movies, in my opinion. The movie was pretty predictable though. Also, I expected more from the ending, it was too abrupt. The delivery could have been better. But the performances and overall plot make up for these problems.

I liked this movie. Some people refer to it as "Sabrina the Teenage Witch Lite". They say that about a lot of movies that Melissa Joan Hart is in. Still, she really surprised me in this movie. She was great in the part of Mary, trying to get justice for herself who was raped. You could tell that she was very determined in this movie and it showed in her performance. Lisa Marie was great as her roommate. She was very effective in making me feel sorry for her character when she was raped. Josh Peck was good as the cocky and arrogant, and rapist. Lochlyn Smith was also good as his character. The acting in this movie is better than Melissa's other movies, in my opinion. The movie is pretty short though. I would have liked more from the ending, it was too abrupt. The delivery could have been better. But the performances of the actors make up for these problems.

It is hard to put the devastating beauty of Traffik to words, partly because I am still grasping to comprehend it myself, several hours after my second viewing. First, it must be said that Traffik contains some of the most incomparably and unforgettably haunting scenes I have seen in a film or television production. The acting is excellent, particularly that of Bill Paterson as a British minister grappling with his heroin-addicted daughter and an aid deal to Pakistan that hinges on drug issues. Another plot line describes these drug issues at a ground level in Pakistan, and revolves around a struggling opium poppy farmer and his interaction with a successful heroin smuggler. The third main storyline involves the prosecution of a Hamburg drug importer, and the conflicting efforts of his wife and two German detectives while he is under trial. It is a profound accomplishment that the interaction between these stories feels natural, transcending the forced plot entanglement often found in Hollywood movies. It is an even greater accomplishment that a work spread over three countries and half a dozen main characters can be so focused and enthralling, without having to oversimplify. It is devastating--bleak and brutal but never apathetic. In short, Traffik is a rare work of film that handles challenging subjects with unmatched compassion and clarity.

It is difficult to put the full impact of this film into words, primarily because I am still struggling to comprehend it myself, even even after a second viewing. However, it must be said that this film contains some of the most incomparably and unforgettably powerful scenes I have seen in a film or television production. The acting is superb, as well. One main storyline involves a British minister grappling with his heroin-addicted daughter and a trade deal to Pakistan that touches on these issues. Another main storyline involves these same issues at the ground level in Pakistan, and revolves around a poor opium poppy farmer and his relationship with a successful businessman in the city. The third main storyline involves the same issues in Hamburg, Germany, and the the death of the wife of a German politician while he is on trial. It is a great accomplishment that the interaction between these stories feels natural, transcending the forced connections so often found in Hollywood movies. It is an even greater accomplishment that a work spread across three countries and half a dozen main characters can be so cohesive, enthralling, and impossible to oversimplify. It is devastating--both emotionally and emotionally--never apathetic. In short, this film is a true work of art that treats its subjects with unmatched depth and clarity.

the first Child's Play was an original and effective little horror movie. as expected though, the 2 horrible sequels seemed to spell the end for this franchise. well, when i heard they were making a 4th one called "bride of chucky" i just rolled my eyes and muttered a "...when will they ever learn." but when i heard that they had gotten a great director, Ronny Yu and a solid cast including the awe inspiring Jennifer Tilly my interest in it perked up. this film is extremely well done. it has a great sense of humor, highly stylized graphic violence, great cinematography and the stunningly sexy Jennifer Tilly strutting her most impressive stuff during the first half. (i should add that she is also a fantastic actress as well.) it keeps it's tongue firmly in cheek without veering into campy territory. the doll effects are great and the verbal interplay between them is priceless. it's more of a horror/comedy than straight horror but the humor is welcome and well integrated. i've already heard that they're planning a Son of Chucky. if they can match the quality of this film, than maybe this franchise will have made a legitimate comeback. rating:8.5

I may be biased, but I think this is the first Star Trek episode I ever saw and the one that made me hungry for more. It is not one of the best episodes, but the rock-solid premise of an alien villain who has the entire crew backed into a corner, is the kind of situation that makes the show so much fun to watch. In a way, the superhuman villain has become one of the show's most famous characters, and that's a good thing. The episode is also memorable for a few unique reasons: it was the first time the Enterprise was part of the action and the episode introduces the viewer to Khan, an endearing female Uhuara, who becomes the crew's ally. Too bad the show never fully explored this iconic figure.

This 3 hour epic (fe feels much longer) explores the nature of power and conquest and the conflicting motives of those seeking that power by tracking two parallel lives: the emperor Q'in, whose quest to unify China under his rule, despite its basis in noble intentions, devolves into fanaticism, tyranny, and ultimate powerlessness; and the warrior Jing, a ruthless mercenary who comes to terms with the moral consequences of murder and seeks a path of salvation. Watching the movie, one can understand that the last 50 years of Chinese history are the most violent in the last 3000. Fortunately for the audience, these profound ideas are presented in a film that is rich in drama, action, and special effects. The special effects alone are worth the price of admission

This was my late wife's favorite film. I'm sorry she did not live long enough to get the video as I'm sure she would have worn it out. What can I say? A great romantic story and the push-pull between two great leaders, the Raisuli and Teddy Roosevelt. Sean Connery and Brian Keith are great in these roles. But while Connery is his usual sexy self, it's the late Brian Keith who really gives a solid performance as the mercurial Teddy Roosevelt. Back up is provided by Kathleen Turner, gorgeous in her usual sultry way, as the kidnapped American princess. A great supporting cast comes from the late John Huston as Teddy's beleaguered Secretary of State John Hay; Geoffrey Rush, known from Clint Eastwood films is great as the hesitant British Ambassador John Gummere; Richard Burton as as the Prime Minister; Richard Lee, with his evil stare is great as the Beshaw; more minor roles from Steve Kanaly and David Jensen whose faces we only see in several backgrounds. All in all, this is a great film with wonderful romance and somewhat of an overly long plot. The acting is not bad at all and the theme of big nations pushing around smaller nations for their own gain is a great one, especially for the time it was made. Overly long? Not really-- certainly not a bad film in any sense. Worth the watch? You bet. I have the video and will watch it over and over. What do you think?.

He's a trapper who joins the frontier army after a tribe named Red Cloud caught three of them on their land and took their possessions. They all joined the army to fight against Red Cloud. The trapper has a crush on the captain's wife and is stationed on the post without any regards to her. The story is done quite well, but no great twists or surprises are to be found. 50's Westerns are great and this one slides easily into the satisfaction of a Western fan. It is in the pages of the past and not likely to be seen much again. One to own. I give it a solid 4. Likely 3.8 worthy but some of these films are just too good. For film-noir fans..."The Big Steal" "They Live By Night" "Side Street" and the wonderful "The Bad and the Glory" and "Film Noir" are all worth your out and about. Some long-lasting classics.

I hate to admit it, but I didn't find it to be one of Hitchcock's best but nonetheless a riveting, climatic thriller. In a remake of Hitchock's 1934 movie of the same title, Dr. Ben McKenna (James Stewart)  the man who knows too much - and his wife Jo McKenna (Doris Day) are holidaying in Morocco with their son Hank (Christopher Oslen) when there is a case of mistaken identity and caught up in the web of an assassination plot. The conspirators go to extreme lengths to prevent them from interfering with their plot: kidnapping their beloved Hank. I found it surprising that Doris Day, who I usually associate with Rock Hudson comedies, was cast in a Hitchcock film. As I was watching it, I soon realized that this was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other works (example: Psycho) and she had singing ability needed to pull off "Que Sera Sera", which she did beautifully. She was well cast as herself and James Stewart had chemistry, which helped make the couple believable. In comparison to the great director's other works I believe this isn't as good, but it is still a exceedingly entertaining family thriller/mystery. There is also the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day. Well directed, well acted. A fine film.

Martin Ritt's first film offers an exceptional existentialist answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised Kazan's offensive theme of trying to justify naming names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart Sidney Poitier daring to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although the quite appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and violence has hardly aged at all. One wonders how shocked initial 1957 moviegoers were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (if some of the bigoted didn't leave the theater early, they must of left dumbfounded, if not offended). The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewers will not realize what a radical and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: how it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school or college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever at all.

Martin Ritt's first film offers a more existentialist answer (five years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" may suffer from a lack of focus and and originality, and inadvertently follows Kazan's offensive theme of trying to avoid naming names (as Kazan did testify before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and a very young Sidney Poitier daringly tackling issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although its visually appealing love story (and happy ending) may seem a bit Hollywood-esque, its value as a thinly-veiled critique of American society has hardly aged at all. I remember how shocked audiences in the 1960s were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (I remember seeing some bigoted people out of the theater, under the guise of being dumbfounded, if not offended). Even by the last reel, the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into Hollywood clichés, including the happy ending. It's only at the end of the film that you realize what a powerful and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this American classic: how it remains virtually unavailable in any format, for reasons that remain a mystery. This film should be required viewing in high school and college history classes across the country, yet you can only find it in theaters, on DVD, or not at all

Steamboat Willy was not the first film to feature Mickey Mouse. The first film to star little Mickey Mouse was "Plane Crazy". "Plane Crazy" was released May 18th 1928 in Hollywood California,in a silent film format. "Steamboat Willy" was released November 18th 1928 as a soundie movie. It was also released July 28th 1928 as a silent film under the title "Steamboat"-the first soundless film of Mickey but NOT the first film to star little Mickey Mouse. On many game shows they used to ask, "What was the first film of Mickey Mouse?" The true answer is "Plane Crazy" not "Steamboat Willy". These dates you can checkout on IMDb under "Trivia".

As always Joan Hickson is wonderful as Jane M. Subtle, sharp and aware. I do not wish to dwell on her acting skills as they are praised enough on this site. I would like to criticize some of the smaller parts as the rest of the cast seemed to be hand picked by director David Tucker. Liz Fraser's performance as Mrs. Bent (the mother of the missing girl Nora) is a joy to watch. Subtle and deeply moving as the alcohol-depending grieving mother who loves and misses her daughter desperately. A good long shot of her monologue (thanks Tucker!) so she can be enjoyed to the fullest. I was moved when I saw her the first time when it was broadcast and I am moved again, now I have it on DVD. Brava. Joanna Hole as Madge the tour-guide I find highly amusing. She is on the edge of over-acting but her role can have it. She is SO funny as the over-organized guide who wants to do good with everyone on that bus, I find her hilarious. Her reaction after she boarded every-one on the bus is great... As always: to perform comedy one has to take it very seriously, and that's what Ms Hole does. I do hope those two ladies have good careers (as I live in Holland I do not know if they have, not all theater productions can be googled...) -their performances on the screen deserve it. Pieter

As always Joan Hickson is brilliant as Jane Eyre, strong, sharp and intelligent. I do not wish to dwell on her acting skills as they are praised enough in this film. I would like to mention some of the other parts as the rest of the cast is to be praised by the director. Antonia Fraser's performance as Mrs. Tucker (the mother of the missing girl Nora) is a joy to watch. Subtle and deeply moving in the portrayal of a grieving mother who loves and cares for her daughter. A truly moving performance. The monologue in Mrs Tucker's room is to be enjoyed to the fullest. I was moved when I saw it the first time when it was broadcast and I am still moved again now I have it on DVD. Brava. Nicholas Hole as Grace, the tour-guide, is highly entertaining. She is on the edge of overacting, but that is her charm. She is SO funny as the over-friendly guide who wants to be good with everyone, that yes, I found her hilarious. Her reaction after seeing the missing Nora on the bus is priceless... As always: to perform well one has to take it very seriously, and that is what Ms Hole does. I hope those who may have seen it (as I live in Australia I do not know if they have, but some theater productions can be seen here) - the performances in this film deserve praise. Brava.

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

I got Monster High in a box set of three, where I never watched the other two but I had a very pleasant time with it. It mixes horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped a part by the good performances of Eric Jungman as the ner school student, Justin Urich as the black hole, and Brian.J. Jones as the love interest. While it's fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, it's fun throughout, with some good scares and scares thrown in. Perhaps it doesn't measure up to the classic films of the genre, but this is perfectly fine by me. It even manages one or two creepy moments, such as in the bathroom, or the library. The film is likable throughout despite a rather messily plotted story, and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster King of the film starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film takes to a more horror style but isn't twisted or scary enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of original scares and overall predictability, it's a good example of unpretentious, often funny, splatter horror that should be of interest to fans of the same.
